4.12: LOLITALOLITA is a 1955 novel written by Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov that addresses the controversial subject of hebephilia. The protagonist is a French literature professor who moves to New England and writes under the pseudonym Humbert Humbert. He describes his obsession with a 12-year-old ‘nymphet’, Dolores Haze, whom he kidnaps and sexually abuses after becoming her stepfather. Privately, he calls her "Lolita", the Spanish diminutive for Dolores. 4.17: What is POV?Definition: Point of view can generally be defined as (p.83)1)who tells the story2) how the stories are told or the way in which it is narrated.Point of view is the outlook on the action that the reader will follow. It is decided by the author and it controls largely what the reader will see and know (p.7) Point of view signifies the way, a story gets told— the mode established by an author by means of which the reader is presented with the characters, dialogue, action settings, and events which constitute the narrative in a work of fiction (2014:301).
4.18: What is POV?Types: 1) First-person point of view/personal narration2) Second-person point of view 3) Third person point of view a. “I” -----the author [e.g. autobiography] b. “I” -----a central character c. “I” -----a fortuitous witness and auditor d. “I”-----a participant but only a minor onea. “an inverted first person POV”/the narrator in the storyb. “You” referring to the reader c. “You” referring to a specific character a. objective point of view b. omniscient point of viewc. Limited omniscient point of view
4.19: First-Person POV: I / WeDefinitionIt is perspective used in narrative. The Narrator, “I”, can be the author or one of the characters (p.83) The narration usually utilizes the pronoun I (or we, if the narrator is speaking as part of a group). It also means that impressions and descriptions are colored by that character’s opinions, mood, past experiences, or even their warped perceptions of what they see and hear.
4.20: First-Person POV: I / WeTypes “I” could be “the central character”——Jane Eyre in Jane Eyre “I” could be the author———Benjamin Franklin in his autobiography and Lincoln Steffens in ‘I Become a Student’ “I” could be “a fortuitous witness and auditor of the matters he or she relates”——Marlow in Heart of Darkness“I” could be “a participant, but only a minor or peripheral one”——Nick in The Great Gatsby

4.38: Third-Person POV: He/She/It/They Omniscient point of view: The narrator knows everything that needs to be known about the agents, actions, and events and has privileged access to the characters’ thoughts, feelings, and motives; also that the narrator is free to move at will in time and space, to shift from character to character, and to report (or conceal) their speech, doings, and states of consciousness (2014:301-2)/(p.87). The author is godlike, seeing and knowing all. The author tells the reader about the thought processes of each character without worrying about how the information is obtained. (p.7)Definition:

5.8: Ambrose Bierce-Hare and Tortoise A Hare having ridiculed the slow movements of a Tortoise, was challenged by the latter to run a race, a Fox to go to the goal and be the judge. They got off well together, the hare at the top of her speed, the Tortoise, who had no other intention than making his antagonist exert herself, going very leisurely. After sauntering along for some time he discovered the Hare by the wayside, apparently asleep, and seeing a chance to win pushed on as fast as he could, arriving at the goal hours afterward, suffering from extreme fatigue and claiming the victory.  "Not so," said the Fox; "the Hare was here long ago, and went back to cheer you on your way."
5.9: Ambrose Bierce-Hare and Tortoise Unlike the traditional tale where the hare's arrogance and overconfidence lead to his defeat, this version highlights the hare's awareness and sportsmanship. The hare not only wins the race but also shows humility by returning to cheer on the tortoise. Meanwhile, the tortoise's slow pace and eventual fatigue emphasize the limits of perseverance when it is not matched with a realistic understanding of the situation.1. True success is not just about winning but about showing kindness and humility, uplifting others even in moments of triumph2. Perseverance alone is not enough; it must be paired with a realistic understanding of one's limitations and the situation to achieve true success.

5.11: What is THEME?DEFINITIOONIt is the underlying meaning of a story and embodies general truths about society or human nature. (p.7)The theme is the central meaning of the narrative. It has been called the worldview, philosophy, message, or moral lesson within a story. (p.109)A theme connects a profound idea about our world to the events within a text. It reflects the central concept you wish to share with your readers, one that has the potential to inspire, provoke thought, and transform perspectives.
5.12: What is THEME?DEFINITIOONMost modern critics of prose fiction, whatever their persuasion, make an important distinction between the fictional scenes, persons, events, and dialogue that a narrator reports or describes and the narrator’s own assertions about the world, about human life, or about the human situation; the central or controlling, generalization of the latter sort are said to be the theme or thesis of the work (2014:129)
5.13: THEME ≠ TOPICS /Main Idea/Summary Morals/Truth➡️
5.14: What is THEME?Significance The theme is the most important thing the author wants the reader to get from the story (p.109) Themes are one of the most fundamental aspects in narrative writing (p.115) Themes provide the foundation on which a story rests and themes are the soil from which all stories grow. (p.115)
5.15: What are COMMON TOPICS for THEMEs?The Coming of AgeNostalgia LonelinessRedemption Love Sacrifice Betrayal Loyalty GreedJustice Oppression Revenge Hatred Conflict: Man vs. Society Conflict: Man vs. Nature Conflict: Man vs. Oneself Conflict: Man vs. Technology

5.169: Figurative Language: UnderstatemenDefinition:Understatement is a figure of speech in which something is expressed less strongly than would be expected, or in which something is presented as being smaller, worse, or lesser than it really is. Typically, understatement is used to call attention to the very quality it pretends to downplay.
5.170: Figurative Language: UnderstatemenDefinition:1)Understatement is a figure of speech. Understatement deliberately makes a situation less important or serious than it is (p.131). 2)It deliberately represents something as very much less in magnitude or importance than it really is, or is ordinarily considered to be. The effect is usually ironic (2014:167).
5.171: 1. Understatement is generally intended to be humorous.2. However, the use of understatement can also be modest or polite, since it can downplay things that it would be boastful or inappropriate to say directly.3. Comedic understatement is a form of verbal irony[sarcasm], since the literal meaning of what someone says is different from what they actually mean.

6.13: What is PLOT?Definition: Plot is a series of events and thoughts arranged to reveal their dramatic and emotional significance. Plot is not just a sequence of chronological events. Rather, plot implies that there is a meaningful relationship among the events. Feature: Plot is often characterized by a conflict, a struggle between two or more opposing forces. The conflict may be internal or external. The story may have more than one conflict (p.139).Five Elements of Plot: Exposition-Rising Action-Climax-Falling Action-Resolution/DenouementThe plot in a dramatic or narrative work is constituted by its events and actions, as these are rendered and ordered toward achieving particular artistic and emotional effects (2014:293).

6.16: What is the Role of CONFLICT?Conflict is the key to plotting a great script. It defines the parameters of the story, helps to generate tension and suspense and shapes the audience experience of the characters (p.144-145)Suspense in ConflictThe Main ConflictCharacters in ConflictEvery plot needs a main conflict for the protagonist to face. This conflict defines the basic parameters of the plot and raises the dramatic question of the story that is answered at the climax. It contains the protagonist’s main objective and the main obstacle (p.145)The characters involved in a conflict are rival characters which usually contrast with each other. However, opposing characters aren’t always antagonists; sometimes, they just present opposing ideas (p.145).The sort of suspense created by conflict is “Willy Wonty”, the readers’ uncertainty as to whether a character “will” or “won’t” commit an act, decide a matter, or do a deed (p.145)

It is the act of leaving out one or more words that are not necessary for understanding.
